implementation_notes: The creation owner is a static factory method on the aggregate - Order.FromCart(cart), Order.Rehydrate(row) - that validates and returns the object while the constructor stays private or internal so call sites cannot skip it; Microsoft's framework design guidance prefers a simple constructor for the common case and explicitly allows static factory methods when the construction semantics differ from construction. A separate factory class is warranted only when creation needs injected collaborators, and required/init-only members (C# 11/9) let the compiler force all mandatory state to be set during construction instead of validating afterwards. For application components the container (IServiceProvider, ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance) is the creation owner; keep domain-object creation out of the container so the model stays persistence- and DI-ignorant.
pitfalls: A private constructor is not enough: object initializers on mutable members, record with expressions and serializers can all produce instances outside the factory, so keep invariant-bearing state immutable or validate in the accessors.
Static factories are less discoverable than constructors (no new-IntelliSense); if creation is the core scenario, keep a simple constructor and let the factory cover only the special paths.
Async factories are a smell: constructors cannot be async, and a Task<Order> factory invites callers to observe a partially initialized object; load collaborators first and construct synchronously.

variants.name: Container-owned creation (ActivatorUtilities / registered factory delegate)
variants.implementation_notes: When the aggregate's collaborators come from the application container, the creation owner can be a registered factory delegate (AddTransient<Func<Cart, Order>>(sp => ...)) or ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<Order>(sp, raw), which resolves constructor arguments from the provider and mixes in call-site arguments. This is the right owner for application components; for aggregates it should stay a thin adapter that calls the domain-side factory method instead of moving validation into DI.
pitfalls: ActivatorUtilities creates instances the container does not track: do not mix it with scoped services or disposable lifetimes you expect the container to manage.
A factory delegate that resolves from a captured scope pins that scope open for the delegate's lifetime (captive dependency).
Registering the aggregate itself as a service invites resolving an Order from DI and blurs the domain/persistence boundary.
